story.moon-air.title: Build your Moon-base air
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.hook.public: Things that are safe on the space station can burn in Moon-base air.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.compare.pub: These highlighted dots are the real tests closest to Moon-base air. None of them were burned in Moon gravity.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.compare.ast: Air-cooled racks need about 80 % more airflow at 8.2 psia (ICES-2022-45).
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.compare.ana: Lunar-gravity oxygen margins run from 0.32 to 2.3 percentage points by material (ICES-2025-392, Table 2). Polycarbonate and Nomex Velcro measured less flammable in lunar gravity.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.compare.ann: None of the tests in NASA's PSI archive ran in Moon gravity.
story.why-oxygen.title: Why oxygen matters
story.why-oxygen.question: Why should anyone care about fire and oxygen?
story.why-oxygen.why-oxygen-main.hook.pu: In January 1967, a fire broke out inside an Apollo spacecraft during a test on the ground. The crew of three died.
story.why-oxygen.why-oxygen-main.hook.as: Apollo 1, 27 January 1967, a ground test: the cabin held 100 % oxygen at pressure. The fire likely began with arcing wires, and the hatch could not open under pressure.
Apollo's cabin held 100 % oxygen. In 1997, a fire on the Mir space station began in a machine that makes oxygen.

What changed after Apollo 1: a quick-opening hatch, restricted materials and fire-resistant suits. Mir, 23 February 1997: an oxygen generator fire filled the station with smoke, and flames blocked one Soyuz.
story.why-oxygen.why-oxygen-main.takeawa: NASA looked at its worst spacecraft fires. All of them happened where there was extra oxygen.
NASA's own review (ICES-2020-173): "All of the most serious events were in the presence of enhanced oxygen." Of 10 loss-of-crew events, 2 involved fire, both in ground tests, both in high oxygen.
story.what-nasa-tested.title: What NASA has tested
story.what-nasa-tested.question: What do we actually know, and how do the tests compare?
story.what-nasa-tested.what-nasa-tested-: NASA lights fires in space to learn. Each dot is one real test. Dots sit higher when the air had more oxygen, and further right when the air pressure was higher.
First, drops of fuel burning in space. NASA ran 369 of these tests.
FLEX (PSI-69): 274 runs, each recorded as Extinction, Disruption or Completion. FLEX-2 adds 8 tests and CFI adds 87.
Next, flames fed by a jet of gas. This is the biggest group, with 1,129 tests. Each dot is one test where NASA wrote down the air.
CFI-G (PSI-159): 179 normal and 154 inverse flames, 333 tests. Flame Design (PSI-10) has 327 tests. SPICE (PSI-107) has 469 but records no oxygen or air pressure, so it is listed, not placed.
Then, solid materials burning in a duct of moving air. 251 tests are listed here, but none is a dot, because nobody wrote down the air pressure.
BASS-II (PSI-25): 129 tests with oxygen recorded. BASS (PSI-26): 122 tests with no oxygen recorded. Neither records air pressure, so no test can be placed.
Then, large fires on big samples, such as fabric. The 17 tests are listed here too, but none is a dot: nobody wrote down the air pressure.
SAFFIRE-I burned a large sample of SIBAL fabric for 420 s at about 21.6 % oxygen and 20 cm/s airflow (PSI-98, row 1).
SAFFIRE I-III: 17 rows. Oxygen is recorded in 11 of them and air pressure in none, so none can be placed.
Then, smoke. These are the only tests here on spotting smoke. All 117 are listed, but none is a dot: nobody wrote down the air pressure.
SAME and SAME-R are the only smoke detection tests in the PSI archive.
SAME-R (PSI-101) has 109 tests and SAME (PSI-102) has 8. Flow speed is recorded in most rows, but no row has oxygen or air pressure.
Last, four studies that rely on computer models and work on the ground. They list no tests, so none of them is a dot.
PSI-60, PSI-62, PSI-117 and PSI-142 each have a test count of 0 in the archive.
Side by side, only the drop and gas-flame tests have dots. The rest are listed, but they have no dot.
One table for every family. Each study recorded the same thing in its own way: oxygen as "Percent O2", "XO2 (init)" or a mole fraction, and pressure in mmHg, atm or bar.
So the tests are real, but only some are dots on the chart. Next, the air a Moon base would have.
story.moon-air.question: Is a Moon base inside or outside the tested evidence?
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.reveal.publ: Earth's air has 21 % oxygen. NASA's plan for a Moon base has 34-40 %, at a bit over half of Earth's pressure. That yellow box is the planned Moon-base air.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.reveal.anal: ISS cabin: 101.4 kPa, 21 % O2. HEO-DM-1006 (8.2 psia): 56.5 kPa, 33.7-40 % O2; maximum O2 36-40 % with control bands.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.focus.publi: Three real spacecraft-scale fires, called Saffire VI, burned close to Moon-base air. They are the hollow marks, and they come from a paper, not from NASA's data archive.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.focus.analy: Saffire VI paper burns: 54.1 kPa at 31.0 % O2, 54.6 at 30.3, 55.2 at 28.8 (NTRS 20250002675, not in PSI). The 10.2 psia exploration air (70.3 kPa, 26.5-30 % O2) is also marked.
story.moon-air.moon-air-main.interactive: Now it is your turn. Drag the two sliders and see how far the nearest real tests are from the air you pick.
At NASA's planned 8.2 psia (56.5 kPa) with 33.7-40 % oxygen, many materials used on the space station are unlikely to pass the flammability test, Nomex among them.
The 10 nearest real PSI tests to the chosen air, each with its distance, recorded outcome and source link.

story.the-gap.title: What nobody knows yet
story.the-gap.question: What must still be tested before people live there?
story.the-gap.the-gap-main.gap.public: None of the tests in NASA's PSI archive ran in Moon gravity. The first fire experiment in real Moon gravity (FM2) is planned for late 2026.
story.the-gap.the-gap-main.gap.astronaut: No fire tests in Moon or Mars gravity are in PSI. NASA calls partial gravity "a major gap" and warns that 1-g limits "may not be conservative" (ICES-2020-173). Smoke mixes through the whole cabin, so alarms can lag while hazardous gases build first.
story.the-gap.the-gap-main.gap.analyst: Missing from PSI: partial-gravity tests, the Saffire IV to VI tables (papers only) and Li-ion fire data.
story.the-gap.the-gap-main.gap.annotatio: None of the tests in NASA's PSI archive ran in Moon gravity.
No PSI combustion tests in partial (lunar or Martian) gravity. FM2 will burn 4 solid samples in real lunar gravity, planned late 2026.
